extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on legal standards that affect public relations practice, including libel, privacy torts, online reputation management, defenses, and litigation public relations. Intended to help PR practitioners and students understand legal risks and appropriate preventive and responsive actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined as a communication that injures another’s reputation or good name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core element plaintiffs must show for a libel action; see Black's Law for legal definition and case law for application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs must prove that the defamatory language is 'of or concerning' them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification can occur without naming (e.g., a job description). Careless reporting that names the wrong person is a common cause of libel suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The defamatory language was witnessed by a third party besides the plaintiff and the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-media defendants only one witness is necessary; for mass media defendants publication is presumed. Publication can occur in PR brochures, newsletters, fiction, yard signs, interoffice memos, conversations, interviews, business letters, e-mail, websites, etc. Anyone who repeats the libelous statement can also be sued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fault
rubrics_metrics.description: A mistake was made; the degree of fault required depends on who is suing whom and the content of the alleged defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fault is a multi-tiered standard (see Actual Malice vs. Negligence) and is central to determining liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual Malice
rubrics_metrics.description: The defamatory statement was made with knowledge that it was false or with 'reckless disregard' to its truthfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A higher burden of proof, generally required when plaintiffs are public officials and public figures (New York Times v. Sullivan). Punitive damages require proof of actual malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negligence (in libel)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defamatory statement was made because the defendant failed to act as a 'reasonable person' would have in similar circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include failure to verify statements or to check court records. This lower burden generally applies to private-figure plaintiffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsity
rubrics_metrics.description: The defamatory language is untrue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The falsity standard generally applies to public officials and public figures; truth is a primary defense but can be difficult to prove definitively in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages (libel)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defamatory language hurt the plaintiff; includes compensatory and punitive damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensatory damages compensate actual financial harms; punitive damages are for non-financial harms (e.g., emotional distress) and require proof of actual malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Legal Persons — Public Officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Government employees who have, or appear to have, substantial responsibility or decision-making control in governmental affairs; can be elected or appointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all government employees qualify; those subject to greater public scrutiny (e.g., city tax assessor, county medical examiner) are public officials and are held to a higher actual-malice standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Legal Persons — Public Figures
rubrics_metrics.description: People who invite attention and comment and thus voluntarily expose themselves to increased public scrutiny (e.g., movie stars, sports figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public figures face higher fault standards (actual malice) and thereby have a greater burden in libel actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Legal Persons — Private Figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals considered more vulnerable to reputational injury and thus afforded a lower standard of fault in libel cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private figures usually need only prove negligence rather than actual malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of Limitations (libel)
rubrics_metrics.description: A libel lawsuit can fail if filed after the state's statute of limitations has expired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes of limitations vary by state, generally ranging from one to three years; counsel should check specific state law timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretrial Remedy — Summary Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge can issue summary judgment in favor of the defendant if the plaintiff fails to meet the libel action’s burden of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary judgment dismisses the case before trial; plaintiffs must have evidence for all elements to avoid dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense — Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving that the allegedly defamatory statements are literally true is a defense to libel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although truth is a defense, it can be difficult to marshal sufficient evidence; credibility of witnesses and availability of proof are practical issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense — Fair Comment / Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment in question was simply an opinion, which is protected as free speech under the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fair comment typically applies more to public officials and public figures; factual assertions disguised as opinion may not be protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense — Privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection invoked when allegedly defamatory language was a fair and accurate report of something that occurred in a government proceeding or document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used by media defendants reporting on government proceedings or documents; privilege may be absolute or qualified depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy Tort — Intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrusion upon the plaintiff’s seclusion or solitude, or into his/her private affairs; deals with how information was gathered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most cases involve media intrusion into people’s lives; actionable even if no publication occurs if the intrusion is highly offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy Tort — Public Disclosure of Private Facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Public disclosure of embarrassing private facts about the plaintiff; concerns sharing information regardless of how it was obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of truthful but private, highly embarrassing information can be actionable if not newsworthy and offensive to a reasonable person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy Tort — False Light
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity that places the plaintiff in a false light in the public eye, often by distorting or fabricating information to suggest someone is other than they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely related to libel; false-light claims often require showing publicity that is offensive and false or highly misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy Tort — Appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage without permission of the plaintiff’s name or likeness for the advantage of the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in commercial contexts (e.g., using someone's image in an ad); consent or license is typically required to avoid liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy Defense — Newsworthiness and First Amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication of some private information is protected by the First Amendment when lawfully obtained from official government records or court proceedings; newsworthiness can outweigh privacy interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The key question is the status of the event as newsworthy, not solely the status of the person; newsworthiness defense applies to stories of public interest and can override privacy concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy Defense — Consent and Model Releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Consent (often via model release) is a defense to privacy claims; releases should be written and state terms explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessary components: written form, names of all parties, scope and duration, and provision for consideration/payment. Ensure the appropriate person signs (minors and mentally disabled persons cannot give legal consent). Implied consent may apply to bystanders who do not move away from public filming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online Reputation — Post with Caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume anything you post is public, even with 'private' security settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat social media posts as potentially permanent and discoverable by employers, clients, or others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online Reputation — Think Long-Term
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how content will reflect on you in 1, 10, or 30 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate posts for future professional and personal consequences before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online Reputation — See it Their Way
rubrics_metrics.description: Look at information or photos from perspectives of parents, employers, clients, or critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how a predisposed reporter or adversary might interpret the content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online Reputation — Patrol the Web
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitor what others post about you and regularly check your online presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up Google Alerts, monitor social media walls, and proactively manage mentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online Reputation — Defend Yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: If inappropriate content is posted about you, request removal and contact hosting platforms if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider takedown requests; exercise caution before hiring reputation-management services; document and escalate through platform procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation Public Relations
rubrics_metrics.description: A specialty practice that helps organizations address interests beyond legal concerns during legal controversies, including impacts on shareholders, employees, customers, and partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigation PR counselors help manage public opinion and nonlegal consequences of lawsuits; organizations should seek both legal and public relations counsel because damage outside the courtroom can exceed legal losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional Conduct — Know Legal Boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners do not practice law, but sound legal knowledge helps them work in partnership with legal personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should avoid performing legal work, cooperate with lawyers, consider malpractice insurance, and remember that private actions (including online behavior) can affect professional reputation and liability.
